subject: Chemistry
title: The Pharaoh's Serpent
description: Learn The Pharaoh's Serpent in one minute.

hook.text: Light mercury thiocyanate and a dark, snake-like column erupts from the tiny pellet, growing like a living thing.

buildup.text: The heat triggers decomposition. Carbon nitride ash expands dramatically as gases push it outward.

discovery.text: The 'serpent' is a foamy carbon structure inflated by nitrogen and sulfur gases escaping the reaction.

twist.text: This used to be sold as a children's firework in the 1800s—until people realized mercury fumes are toxic.

climax.text: Modern versions use baking soda and sugar. Safer, but the original remains chemistry's creepiest demo.

punchline.text: A pellet becomes a dark serpent. Chemistry's spookiest trick.

quiz.question: Why was the original Pharaoh's Serpent firework banned?
options: Mercury thiocyanate produces toxic mercury fumes
The snake was too realistic and scared people

details.summary: The Pharaoh's Serpent is a dramatic decomposition reaction where mercury thiocyanate ignites to produce a large, twisting ash structure resembling a serpent. The expanding solid forms as gases escape from the decomposing compound, creating an eerie growing column.
details.whyItMatters: This reaction was once a popular firework but is now banned in many countries due to mercury toxicity. It remains an important historical example of decomposition reactions producing visually striking results.
takeaways: Mercury thiocyanate decomposes into an expanding ash serpent
The reaction releases toxic mercury vapor and is no longer sold
Modern versions use safer compounds like sodium bicarbonate

faq.question: Why was the Pharaoh's Serpent firework eventually banned?
faq.answer: The decomposition of mercury thiocyanate releases toxic mercury vapor and hydrogen cyanide gas. Several poisoning cases, particularly among children who handled the pellets, led to bans in most countries by the mid-twentieth century.

faq.question: What is the safe modern alternative to the Pharaoh's Serpent?
faq.answer: The sugar-and-baking-soda snake uses sodium bicarbonate and sugar in sand, ignited with lighter fluid. The heated baking soda decomposes to release CO2, which puffs the caramelizing sugar into a growing black carbon snake without any toxic fumes.
